title: The First Skyscrapers
objective: After this level you can explain how Chicago built the first skyscrapers.
summary: After the 1871 fire, Chicago's Chicago school built the first skyscrapers, 10 to 15 years later. Sullivan (1896): form ever follows function; the Wainwright Building reads like a column.

cards.headline: In 1871, Chicago burned. Within a generation, it was growing up.
cards.body: The Great Chicago Fire began on October 8, 1871. About 300 people died, and roughly one in three Chicagoans lost their home. The city that rose afterward became famous for a brand-new kind of building. But the fire didn't build it. What did?

cards.headline: Not overnight
cards.body: Right after the fire, Chicago rebuilt fast, and the new buildings looked much like the old ones. What changed quickly was the ground itself: within months, a land rush began. The earliest skyscrapers came 10 to 15 years later, 8 to 10 stories tall, with steel frames, elevators and new kinds of foundations. The fire cleared the ground. It took new ideas to build up from it.

cards.headline: The Chicago school
cards.body: Those ideas came from a group of architects and engineers now called the Chicago school: William Le Baron Jenney, Daniel Burnham, John Root, Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan. Together they developed the skyscraper. Jenney designed the Home Insurance Building (1884–85), generally considered the first tall building held up by an iron and steel skeleton: Level 8's frame, taken up high. Chicago has been called the birthplace of modern architecture.

cards.headline: Form ever follows function
cards.body: A frame could stand tall. But what should a tall building look like? In an 1896 essay, Louis Sullivan answered: "form ever follows function." Give the street floor a grand entrance and big openings for shops. Above it, stack the offices, and since every office is alike, make every window alike, "because they are all alike." Then top it with an attic that shows the offices have ended. The outside tells you what's inside.

cards.fact: The Wainwright Building reads like a classical column.
cards.context: Critics of the day compared a tall building to a column: base, shaft and capital. Adler and Sullivan's 10-story Wainwright Building in St. Louis (1890–91) fits: a two-story stone base, seven stories of unbroken brick piers, and a leafy frieze under an overhanging roof. Sullivan stressed the upright lines and played down the horizontal ones, so your eye runs straight up.

mascot.line: Squint at it and an office block turns into a classical column. Architecture loves a good disguise.

questions.prompt: In his 1896 essay on the tall office building, what did Louis Sullivan say to do with the windows of the office floors?

options.label: Make each floor's windows different, for variety
options.rationale: He said the opposite: alike, because the offices are alike.

options.label: Make them all alike, because the offices are all alike
Leave the office floors windowless, for strength
options.rationale: Offices need windows; he made them identical.

options.label: Make the top floors' windows the biggest
options.rationale: The attic, not the offices, marks the top.

questions.explanation: Sullivan wrote that the office tiers should look alike "because they are all alike": form ever follows function.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to say the 1871 fire instantly gave Chicago its first skyscrapers?

options.label: Chicago banned new building for 20 years
options.rationale: A land rush began within months.

options.label: The first skyscrapers had been built before the fire
options.rationale: They came after it, not before.

options.label: The fire only burned the city's suburbs
options.rationale: The card is about rebuilding, not where it burned.

options.label: The earliest skyscrapers came 10 to 15 years later

questions.explanation: Right after the fire, new buildings looked like the old ones; skyscrapers with steel frames and elevators followed 10 to 15 years later.

questions.prompt: Level 8's frame idea went tall in Chicago. Which Chicago school building is generally considered the first tall building on an iron and steel skeleton?

options.label: The Wainwright Building
options.rationale: That's Sullivan's St. Louis tower of 1890-91.

options.label: The Crystal Palace
options.rationale: That was an iron and glass exhibition hall in London.

options.label: The Empire State Building
options.rationale: That came in 1931, in New York.

questions.explanation: Jenney's Home Insurance Building (1884-85) is generally considered the first tall building held up by an iron and steel skeleton.
